Appendix A — Find the next useful command

1. Appendix A — Find the next useful command

A command is useful when its output separates two plausible explanations. Start with the question, choose the smallest relevant observation, and compare the result with a stated expectation. These are inspection starting points, not a sequence to run automatically on every host.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Appendix A — Find the next useful command

2. Read the operational contract

Keep the source procedure, its preconditions and its verification together. Follow the named primary documentation for the installed version. A command copied without its surrounding assumptions answers a different question.

SOURCE: Read the operational contract

3. Appendix A — Find the next useful command

A command is useful when its output separates two plausible explanations. Start with the question, choose the smallest relevant observation, and compare the result with a stated expectation. These are inspection starting points, not a sequence to run automatically on every host.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Appendix A — Find the next useful command

4. Identify the environment

cat /etc/os-release identifies the distribution. uname -r identifies the running kernel. systemctl --version identifies the installed systemd tools; it does not by itself prove that this environment boots with systemd. ps -p 1 -o pid,comm,args identifies the visible PID 1. Read Chapters 1, 7, and 8 when those answers seem inconsistent.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Identify the environment

5. Find a path or permission boundary

pwd -P shows the current physical directory. ls -ld PATH inspects the directory entry rather than listing its contents. namei -l PATH traces pathname components where installed. id, getfacl PATH, ls -Z PATH, and the service’s effective configuration reveal different access layers. A user-shell write test is not automatically equivalent to a sandboxed service write. See Chapters 3–5 and 18.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Find a path or permission boundary

6. Understand storage pressure

df -hT reports filesystem block capacity and type. df -i reports inode capacity. du -x -h DIRECTORY accounts for reachable directory entries on one filesystem. findmnt --target PATH identifies the containing mount. lsof +L1 can identify open unlinked files, subject to access and scope. None of these commands alone identifies every cause of a full filesystem. See Chapters 9, 21, 23, and 32.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Understand storage pressure

7. Understand a process

ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,comm shows a selected process view. top samples changing activity. pidstat -u -r -d 1 5 collects bounded process measurements when sysstat is installed. A PID is a current identifier, not a permanent application identity. Check the process start time and owner before signaling a reused number. See Chapters 7 and 22.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Understand a process

8. Understand a systemd service

systemctl status NAME.service --no-pager provides a useful summary. systemctl cat NAME.service shows unit files and drop-ins. systemctl show NAME.service exposes manager properties. journalctl -u NAME.service --since '-10 minutes' retrieves a time-scoped log view. A unit can be active while its application is unhealthy, and an enabled unit can currently be stopped. See Chapters 8, 14, and 23.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Understand a systemd service

9. Trace a network request

ip -br address, ip route, and ip route get DESTINATION answer address and route questions. ss -lntp inspects TCP listeners. getent hosts NAME follows the configured system name-service path; dig NAME asks DNS. curl tests an application request and can validate HTTPS when name and trust are correct. Each test skips or includes different layers. See Chapters 11–13 and 19.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Trace a network request

10. Inspect the installed software

Use rpm -q PACKAGE and dnf info PACKAGE on the RHEL-family baseline. Use dpkg-query and apt-cache policy PACKAGE on the Debian-family baseline. Installed version, repository candidate, and running process code are different facts. Read the proposed package transaction before approving it. See Chapter 6.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Inspect the installed software

11. Inspect access policy without removing it

sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones is appropriate on a firewalld-managed host. sudo nft list ruleset inspects the effective nftables ruleset. getenforce reports SELinux mode; aa-status reports AppArmor information where available. Do not treat these tools as interchangeable configuration managers or disable one to make another test pass. See Chapters 17 and 18.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Inspect access policy without removing it

12. Validate a candidate before applying it

bash -n SCRIPT checks Bash syntax, not behavior. sshd -t validates SSH server configuration, not every user’s ability to log in. nginx -t validates the complete NGINX configuration and some referenced resources, not the entire client path. findmnt --verify --tab-file FILE inspects an fstab candidate, not every future storage condition. A validation command is one gate, followed by application-level verification and recovery planning.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Validate a candidate before applying it

13. Read an error as evidence

Record the exact command, host, identity, timestamp, exit status, and relevant output. Separate a refused connection from a timeout, an absent DNS name from a resolver that cannot answer, a permission denial from a nonexistent path, and a full filesystem from a full directory assumption. These distinctions reduce both wasted effort and dangerous changes.

SOURCE: EPUB/text/ch036.xhtml — Read an error as evidence
